The Idea

Why The Paper Loop?

School campuses throw away huge amounts of written notebook scrap every day. Left in landfills, it releases methane as it breaks down; burned, it releases CO₂ and toxic ash. The Paper Loop de-inks and re-pulps that scrap using only warm water and baking soda — no chlorine bleach — then strengthens it with a natural cornstarch binder so the recycled sheets are smooth, tear-resistant, and ready to write on again.

📓15–20 written notebook sheets
🧂Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate)
🌽Cornstarch (natural binder)
💧Warm & ambient water
🌼Turmeric, beetroot, mustard/marigold seeds
🔧Mixer-grinder, churner, mesh frame, rolling pin
Step by Step

How We Made It

Eight simple stages take written waste paper from classroom scrap to a finished, writable sheet — using only household tools and no synthetic chemicals.

1

Collect & Sort

Gather written notebook scrap and rough sheets from the classroom instead of binning them.

2

Tear into Scraps

Hand-tear sheets into roughly 2 cm pieces to expose fiber edges for faster soaking.

3

Soak & Churn

Submerge scraps in warm water and agitate with a wooden churner (kavvam) for 60 minutes.

4

Alkaline De-Inking

Add 1.5 tsp sodium bicarbonate — the mild alkaline bath loosens ink pigments without bleach.

5

Blend into Pulp

Drain the ink water, then blend the de-inked shreds for 30 seconds into a uniform fiber mush.

6

Split the Batches

Divide the pulp into Batch 1 (plain) and Batch 2, which gets the starch binder.

7

Add Starch Binder

Cook 1 tsp cornstarch in 3 tbsp water until translucent, then blend into Batch 2.

8

Cast, Press & Dry

Pour onto a mesh frame, press under cotton with a rolling pin, iron lightly, then fan-dry.

Proof It Works

Starch Binder vs. Plain Pulp

Standardized 3 cm × 10 cm strips were loaded with deadweights until they tore, confirming the starch gel bridges microscopic fiber gaps.

Batch 1 — Plain Pulp145 g
Batch 2 — Starch Binder390 g
168% stronger tensile load capacity
  • ✓ Zero capillary ink bleed on gel and ballpoint pens
  • ✓ Smooth, compact, sealed surface instead of rough and porous
  • ✓ Folds cleanly without snapping — Batch 1 cracks when creased
  • ✓ Resists a water drop for 40–55 seconds vs. 3–5 seconds
  • ✓ No chlorine bleach — de-inking done with baking soda alone
Impact

Benefits of The Paper Loop

A single school section generates about 1.5 kg of waste paper a month — campus-wide, this process can divert up to 45 kg monthly from dumpsites.

🚯

Diverts Landfill Waste

Keeps written scrap out of landfills and incinerators, cutting methane and CO₂ emissions.

🧪

Zero Toxic Chemicals

Uses baking soda for de-inking instead of chlorine bleach — safe for students to handle.

🏠

Decentralized

No industrial plant or transport needed — runs on a classroom table with household tools.

💰

Zero Cost Materials

Supplies school events with free, sustainable stationery made from scrap already on campus.

🌾

Natural Ingredients

Cornstarch, turmeric and beetroot replace synthetic binders and dyes entirely.

📚

Teaches Circular Economy

Gives students a hands-on model of reduce–reuse–retrieve–redesign–recycle in action.

Beyond the Sheet

What You Can Make With It

The starch-bound paper is strong enough to be cut, layered and finished into real campus products.

🌱

Plantable Seed Paper

Mustard or marigold seeds embedded before drying — plant the bookmark or badge after use.

🎨

Naturally Dyed Sheets

Turmeric gives a golden finish, beetroot extract gives a pastel rose — no synthetic dye.

🏆

Merit Certificates

Layered starch-bound sheets form rigid cardstock for school and Eco-Club awards.

🔑

Upcycled Keychains

Rigid cut-outs with punched eyelets and jute lanyards for school events.

💌

Greeting Cards

Writable, textured cardstock for artistic and commemorative cards.

The Result

Two Batches, One Clear Winner

Fully dried, cured sheets from both batches side by side. Batch 2 — reinforced with the cornstarch binder — came out smoother, stronger and completely writable, proving the hypothesis that a natural polysaccharide gel can replace the strength virgin paper normally gets from long, unbroken cellulose fibers.
